1. Core Clinical Tension: A 34-year-old man presents with recurrent abdominal pain and an expanding thick-walled cystic collection in the body and tail of the pancreas two months after an episode of acute pancreatitis. The core clinical challenge is distinguishing a conventional post-pancreatitis pseudocyst or walled-off pancreatic necrosis from a primary pancreatic hydatid cyst, where misdiagnosis can lead to peroperative cyst rupture, anaphylactic shock, and secondary dissemination.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint is placed upon admission to the surgical department following initial laboratory workup and admission CT scanning demonstrating the 12 × 4 cm pancreatic fluid collection, immediately before the elective surgical exploration and cyst fenestration.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pancreatic pseudocyst is overwhelmingly the most common cystic lesion following acute pancreatitis, typically developing within 4–6 weeks as a thick-walled collection containing amylase-rich fluid. Pancreatic abscess or infected necrosis produces a thick-walled collection with fat stranding and elevated CRP, but aspirated fluid is purulent with bacteria. Pancreatic hydatid cyst is an exceedingly rare presentation (<1% of hydatid cases) whose pathognomonic finding is the aspiration of crystal-clear 'eau de roche' fluid and extraction of multiple viable daughter cysts and germinative endocyst membranes.
case_prompt: A 34-year-old man was admitted to the surgery department complaining of diffuse abdominal pain, dyspnea, generalized fatigue, and progressive weakness. His past medical history was notable for hospitalization at another medical center two months earlier for an episode of acute pancreatitis. On admission, physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. Laboratory investigations were within normal limits except for an elevated C-reactive protein of 18.1 mg/dL and serum amylase of 765 U/L; hepatic function tests were normal, with total bilirubin of 0.64 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 20 IU/L, and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 19 IU/L. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a 5-cm heterogeneous lesion in the body of the pancreas, peripancreatic fluid accumulation, gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and cysts in the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen demonstrated a thick-walled, heterogeneous fluid collection measuring 12 × 4 cm along the body of the pancreas and left colic gutter, accompanied by surrounding adipose tissue infiltration and mild reactive thickening of the adjacent colonic wall, along with a simple left renal cortical cyst.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The leading presumptive diagnosis given the preceding history of acute pancreatitis and a thick-walled retrogastric fluid collection, but intraoperative exploration and needle aspiration revealed crystal-clear fluid rather than turbid pancreatic fluid, and evacuation yielded distinct daughter cysts and endocyst membranes.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The laboratory values were normal, and a primary diagnosis of pancreatic pseudocyst was probable, and the decision of surgical intervention was decided.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the thick-walled retroperitoneal collection, surrounding fat stranding, elevated C-reactive protein, and persistent abdominal pain, but excluded by the absence of systemic sepsis and the non-purulent, clear nature of the aspirated cyst contents.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed heterogeneous collection of fluid with a thick wall of 12 x 4 cm in size along the body of the pancreas and left colic angle (often an abscess or a pseudocyst) with infiltration of adipose tissue around it and mild thickness at the wall of the colon.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive diagnostic pivot occurred intraoperatively during puncture of the retroperitoneal pancreatic mass, which yielded pathognomonic crystal-clear fluid followed by open fenestration and evacuation of multiple daughter cysts and laminated endocyst membrane.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: In puncture, a clear pure liquid was aspirated proposing the existence of a hydatid cyst. Cyst fenestration was performed, and multiple daughter cysts were evacuated; the endocyst membrane was removed (Figure 2).

editor_comments: High clinical utility teaching case. Breakpoint strictly set before elective surgery and operative aspiration. Zero pathogen leaks. Quotes confirmed verbatim from case text.
